beats.text: Eddington did not bin the data he disliked.
beats.note: Dyson, not Eddington, set aside the defocused Sobral astrographic plates, giving a documented reason: the Sun's heat had distorted the mirror, according to David Kennefick.
Arcseconds of starlight bending at the Sun's edge. The 1920 paper by Dyson, Eddington and Davidson notes the Einstein figure is just double the Newtonian one.

beats.name: Arthur Eddington
beats.role: At Principe on 29 May. He took 16 plates, but only 2 gave results, each showing 5 stars. His own figure was 1.61, give or take 0.30.

beats.name: Crommelin and Davidson
beats.role: At Sobral in Brazil. Their 4 inch lens gave 1.98, give or take 0.18 according to Kennefick. The second lens produced blurred images.

beats.context: Gave results at Principe, out of 16 taken, because the sky was never clear. That thin evidence is why the Sobral plates mattered.

beats.text: In 1979 the Sobral plates were measured again.
beats.note: Harvey and Clements found 1.90 for the 4 inch plates and 1.55 for the astrographic plates. Both sit well above Newton's 0.87.

beats.text: Sixty years on, the plates agreed.
